ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Random suffix intercept removed — must know language-as-fixed-effect fallacy
ground_truth.original_snippet: We included two random intercepts, one for subjects and one for suffixes. This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject) + (1|suffix), data, family = "binomial").
ground_truth.modified_snippet: We included a random intercept for subjects. This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject), data, family = "binomial").
ground_truth.description: Removed random intercept for suffixes — 'language as fixed effect fallacy' (Clark, 1973); ignores suffix-level clustering, inflating Type I error

matched_finding.description: The mixed models in Experiments 1 and 2 include only a random intercept for subjects, despite repeated observations across both subjects and items/suffixes. Ignoring item-level random effects in a crossed design inflates Type I error and treats stimuli as fixed. This is especially problematic because the hypotheses concern suffix-level properties and many observations share suffixes. The later eye-tracking models include random intercepts for subjects and suffixes, highlighting inconsistency in analytic rigor across experiments.
matched_finding.quote: We included a random intercept for subjects. This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject), data, family = "binomial").

This counterbalancing procedure helps to ensure that any effects of the congruency variable are not the result of important it...
ground_truth.modified_snippet: List 1 is presented in Appendix D.
ground_truth.description: Removed Latin-square counterbalancing — without it, item properties are perfectly confounded with condition in within-subject design

matched_finding.description: Experiment 1 states there were two lists and each participant saw one list, but does not report how participants were assigned to lists, whether list was balanced across participants, or whether list effects were tested. Similar clarity is lacking for Experiment 3 list assignment.
matched_finding.quote: stimuli were divided into two experimental lists with 40 items per list. Participants saw only one list

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Formula now computes P(suffix|category) not P(category|suffix) — denominator mismatch with definition
ground_truth.original_snippet: For a particular suffix, type diagnosticity is calculated by dividing the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words that contain the suffix.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: For a particular suffix, type diagnosticity is calculated by dividing the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words falling into this category.
ground_truth.description: Changed denominator from P(category|suffix) to P(suffix|category) — this IS specificity, not diagnosticity; collapses the paper's central theoretical distinction

matched_finding.description: The manuscript gives mutually inconsistent definitions of diagnosticity. In the conceptual introduction, diagnosticity is defined as how well a spelling predicts lexical category, which corresponds to P(category | spelling). In the Methods of the computational analysis, type diagnosticity is instead defined as the number of words ending in the suffix and in the category divided by the total number of words in that category, i.e., P(spelling | category). The examples that follow (e.g., -IAN having diagnosticity 0.54 for nouns because 54% of -IAN words are nouns) match P(category | spelling), not the written formula. This is a critical construct-definition error because all subsequent interpretations of diagnosticity depend on which conditional probability was actually computed.
matched_finding.quote: We define diagnosticity as the strength with which a suffix spelling predicts lexical category... For a particular suffix, type diagnosticity is calculated by dividing the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words falling into this category... A suffix like –IAN is present in nouns (magician), as well as in other categories (Amazonian), and so is not particularly diagnostic for nouns (type diagnosticity of 0.54).

ground_truth.modified_snippet: These results therefore suggest that the category information conveyed by suffix spelling is used during sentence integration processes.
ground_truth.description: Deleted entire pre-target word count confound check — the paper acknowledged this confound (significant p<.05 condition difference) and explicitly ruled it out; now the confound is unaddressed

matched_finding.description: In Experiment 3, pretarget word count differs significantly between congruent and incongruent conditions. Even though letter counts were matched, the difference in number of pretarget words can affect parafoveal processing, launch site, and sentence wrap-up, potentially confounding eye-movement differences attributed to congruency.
matched_finding.quote: Note that the number of words pre-target was slightly different across conditions (congruent: 4.75, incongruent: 5.23, t(64) = 2.07, p < 0.05).

ground_truth.description: Removed native speaker and no-learning-difficulties screening — non-native speakers and dyslexic participants would have different suffix-category sensitivity, adding noise and potentially attenuating effects

matched_finding.description: The paper does not report age, sex/gender distribution, native language status, dyslexia/reading impairment exclusion, vision status, or dialect background. These are important for interpreting reading/spelling performance and for replication, especially because suffix pronunciation/spelling relations may vary across dialects.
matched_finding.quote: Participants were 46 undergraduate students at Royal Holloway, University of London.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Diagnosticity→spelling and specificity→reading, but experiments show opposite — inverts entire logic
ground_truth.original_snippet: That is, we hypothesise that diagnosticity, a measure of spelling-to-meaning consistency, would impact on tasks that involve the mapping of print to meaning (i.e. semantic categorisation, reading), while specificity, a measure of meaning-to-spelling consistency, would impact on spelling behaviour.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: That is, we hypothesise that diagnosticity, a measure of spelling-to-meaning consistency, would impact on tasks that involve the production of spelling, while specificity, a measure of meaning-to-spelling consistency, would impact on tasks involving the mapping of print to meaning (i.e. semantic cat...
ground_truth.description: Swapped diagnosticity/specificity task predictions — diagnosticity should predict reading, specificity should predict spelling; reversed mapping inverts the entire experimental logic

matched_finding.description: The paper explicitly assigns diagnosticity to spelling-to-meaning consistency and specificity to meaning-to-spelling consistency, but then immediately predicts the opposite task mappings. If diagnosticity is spelling-to-meaning, it should be relevant for reading/classification; if specificity is meaning-to-spelling, it should be relevant for spelling production. The manuscript states the reverse in one paragraph, contradicting both its own definitions and the experimental predictions stated later. This creates conceptual confusion around the hypotheses and interpretation of experiments.
matched_finding.quote: That is, we hypothesise that diagnosticity, a measure of spelling-to-meaning consistency, would impact on tasks that involve the production of spelling, while specificity, a measure of meaning-to-spelling consistency, would impact on tasks involving the mapping of print to meaning (i.e. semantic categorisation, reading).

ground_truth.modified_snippet: We then examined the slope of the regression equation lm(Hspelling ~ Hphonology).
